# Page 3^page=3
Chapter 7: Tensor Fields 1. Pre lim i nary, 2. Co vari ant dif fer en ti a tion, 3. Christo˙el symbols, 4. Covariant di˙erentiation of tensors, 5. Ricci's theorem, 6. Riemann-Christo˙el tensor, 7. Ricci tensor. 1 35

# Page 4^page=4
Preliminary

# Page 5^page=5
So far So far So far, most bases we considered were independent from the position. For instance, we can take the canonical basis of R3 e1 = (1, 0, 0), e2 = (0, 1, 0), e3 = (0, 0, 1). We see that this is a ˝xed basis and does not depend on any parameter. 2 35

# Page 6^page=6
Vector Fields - Preliminary De˝nition A vector ˝eld assigns a vector to every point in a subset of space. Examples Velocity Field: Represents the velocity of a ˛uid at di˙erent points in space. Gravitational Field: Represents the gravitational force experienced by a mass at di˙erent points in space. Local bases: We could also de˝ne a basis e1(x), e2(x), e3(x) that depends on the position. 3 35

# Page 7^page=7
Derivatives of tensor fields Derivatives of tensor ˝elds We have seen derivatives of tensor ˝elds of rank zero. For instance, Gradient: ∇f = ∇if or ∇iuj = ∂uj ∂xi , Divergence: ∇ · u = ∇iui, Curl: ∇ × u = ϵijk∇juk. Remark. We can also take the derivative of rank 2 tensors such as ∂σjk ∂xi . This is the derivative of the conductivity tensor, which itself is a rank 3 tensor. 4 35

# Page 8^page=8
Covariant differentiation

# Page 9^page=9
Explanation of Covariant Differentiation De˝nition Covariant di˙erentiation is a way to di˙erentiate vectors and tensors in curved space, ensuring the result is still a tensor. Idea Imagine moving a vector along a curved surface. Covariant di˙erentiation adjusts the vector to account for the curvature. 5 35

# Page 10^page=10
Covariant differentiation: Cartesian Coordinates Covariant di˙erentiation: Cartesian Coordinates Consider a Cartesian coordinate system with an orthonormal basis i1, i2, i3, and a vector ˝eld A = A(r) (i.e. a vector that varies in space). Assume the components of A are A1(r), A2(r), A3(r), that is A = A1(r) i1 + A2(r) i2 + A3(r) i3 = Aj(r) ij. Then the di˙erential of A is dA = d(Aj(r) ij) ︸ ︷︷ ︸ product rule = ij dAj(r) + Aj(r)dij. 6 35

# Page 11^page=11
Covariant differentiation: Cartesian Co- ordinates - Part 2 Covariant di˙erentiation: Cartesian Coordinates Again, dA = d(Aj(r) ij) ︸ ︷︷ ︸ product rule = ij dAj(r) + Aj(r)dij. Since the basis i1, i2, i3 does not vary from point to point dij = 0, ∀j. Then the di˙erential of A is dA = ij dAj(r) + Aj(r)dij ︸ ︷︷ ︸ =0 = ij dAj(r) = dA1(r) i1 + dA2(r) i2 + dA3(r) i3 = (dA1(r), dA2(r), dA3(r)). 7 35

# Page 12^page=12
General Coordinates with fixed basis General Coordinates with ˝xed basis Consider a generalised coordinate system with a ˝xed basis e1, e2, e3 (constants). Let A be a vector. We know it can be expanded via A = e 1A1(r) + e 2A2(r) + e 3A3(r) = e1A1(r) + e2A 2(r) + e3A3(r), where A1(r), A2(r), A3(r) are the covariant components and A1(r), A2(r), A3(r) are the contravariant components of A = A(r). Then, the di˙erential of A is dA = d(Aj(r)e j) = e j dAj(r), dA = d(Aj(r)ej) = ej dA j(r), where dej = dej = 0. 8 35

# Page 13^page=13
Generalised Coordinates with local basis Generalised Coordinates with local basis Now, suppose we have a generalised coordinate system with a local basis e1, e2, e3. That is, the basis varies from point to point: ej = ej(x1, x 2, x 3), e j = e j(x1, x 2, x 3). Because e1, e2, e3 is a basis, any vector A = A(r) can be expanded as A = e 1A1 + e 2A2 + e 3A3 = e1A1 + e2A2 + e3A 3. However, it is not true that dej = dej = 0 here. So the di˙erential of A is dA = d(Aje j) = e j dAj + Aj de j, dA = d(A jej) = ej dA j + Aj dej. 9 35

# Page 14^page=14
Vector differential using local basis Vector di˙erential using local basis In a generalised coordinate system with a local basis we have dA = e j dAj + Aj de j, dA = ej dA j + Aj dej. We can also write dA = ∂A ∂xk dxk. We then conclude that the partial di˙erentiation is given by ∂A ∂xk = ∂(Ajej) ∂xk = ∂Aj ∂xk e j + Aj ∂ej ∂xk = ∂(Ajej) ∂xk = ∂Aj ∂xk ej + A j ∂ej ∂xk . 10 35

# Page 15^page=15
Example of Covariant Differentiation Example Consider a generalised coordinate system with local basis e 1 = e 1(x1, x 2, x 3) = 2x1i + x1j + x3k, e 2 = e 2(x1, x 2, x 3) = x2j + x2k, e 3 = e 3(x1, x 2, x 3) = x3k. Find the partial derivative ∂A ∂x1 of the vector A = x2i + 2x 1j + x1x3k. 11 35

# Page 16^page=16
Solution Solution ∂A ∂x1 = ∂Aj ∂x1 e j + Aj ∂ej ∂x1 . Since A = x2i + 2x1j + x1x3k, we have ∂Aj ∂x1 e j = ∂A1 ∂x1 e 1 + ∂A2 ∂x1 e 2 + ∂A3 ∂x1 e 3 = ∂x2 ∂x1 e 1 + ∂2x1 ∂x1 e 2 + ∂x1x3 ∂x1 e 3 = 2 e 2 + x3 e 3. Substituting e2 = x2j + x2k and e3 = x3k, we obtain ∂A ∂x1 = 2(x2j + x2k) + x3(x3k) = 2x2j + (2x2 + (x 3) 2)k. 12 35

# Page 17^page=17
Solution - Part 2 Solution ∂A ∂x1 = ∂Aj ∂x1 e j + Aj ∂ej ∂x1 . The second term is Aj ∂ej ∂x1 = A1 ∂e1 ∂x1 + A2 ∂e2 ∂x1 + A3 ∂e3 ∂x1 = A1 ∂(2x1i + x1j + x3k) ∂x1 + A2 ∂(x2j + x2k) ∂x1 + A3 ∂(x3k) ∂x1 = A1(2i + j) + 0 + 0 = 2A1i + A1j. 13 35

# Page 18^page=18
Solution - Part 3 Solution We want to compute ∂A ∂x1 = ∂Aj ∂x1 e j + Aj ∂ej ∂x1 . We found ∂Aj ∂x1 e j = 2x2j + (2x2 + (x3) 2)k, Aj ∂ej ∂x1 = 2A1i + A1j. Therefore, ∂A ∂x1 = 2x2j + (2x2 + (x 3) 2)k + 2A1i + A1j = 2A1i + (2x2 + A1)j + (2x2 + (x3) 2)k. 14 35

# Page 19^page=19
Partial derivatives are vectors Partial derivatives are vectors One can show that each partial derivative ∂A ∂xk (k = 1, 2, 3) is a vector . To ease notation, let us denote vk = ∂A ∂xk , for k = 1, 2, 3. As any vector, the vector vk also has covariant and contravariant components: Contravariant: vk = (Ak)1e1 + (Ak)2e2 + (Ak)3e3 = (Ak)iei. Covariant: vk = (Ak)1e1 + (Ak)2e2 + (Ak)3e3 = (Ak)iei. For simplicity, we will write Ai ·k = (Ak)i. Ai,k = (Ak)i. 15 35

# Page 20^page=20
Partial derivatives are vectors Partial derivatives are vectors These components Ai ·k and Ai,k are themselves components of a second rank tensor called the covariant derivative . Let us ˝nd a formula for Ai,k. ∂A ∂xk = vk = A1,ke 1 + A2,ke 2 + A3,ke 3. Thus, ∂A ∂xk · ei = vk · ei = (A1,ke 1 + A2,ke 2 + A3,ke 3) · ei = A1,k(e 1 · ei) + A2,k(e 2 · ei) + A3,k(e 3 · ei) = Ai,k. 16 35

# Page 21^page=21
Partial derivatives are vectors Partial derivatives are vectors We have shown Ai,k = ∂A ∂xk · ei. Similarly, we can show Ai ·k = ∂A ∂xk · e i. 17 35

# Page 22^page=22
Summary: Covariant differentiation Summary: Covariant di˙erentiation To summarise covariant di˙erentiation: ∂A ∂xk = ∂Aj ∂xk e j + Aj ∂ej ∂xk = ∂Aj ∂xk ej + Aj ∂ej ∂xk . Ai,k := ∂A ∂xk · ei and Ai ,k := ∂A ∂xk · e i. Putting this together we have Ai,k = ∂A ∂xk · ei = ∂Ai ∂xk + Aj ∂ej ∂xk · ei, A i ,k = ∂A ∂xk · e i = ∂Ai ∂xk + Aj ∂ej ∂xk · e i. 18 35

# Page 23^page=23
Christoffel Symbols

# Page 24^page=24
New notation New notation Again, the covariant derivatives are de˝ned by Ai,k = ∂Ai ∂xk + Aj ∂ej ∂xk · ei, Ai ,k = ∂Ai ∂xk + Aj ∂ej ∂xk · e i We want to simplify these expressions. We will introduce a new symbol for that, which is called Chisto˙el symbol . 19 35

# Page 25^page=25
Christoffel Symbol Christo˙el Symbol Covariant derivatives are de˝ned by Ai,k = ∂Ai ∂xk + Aj ∂ej ∂xk · ei, Ai ,k = ∂Ai ∂xk + Aj ∂ej ∂xk · e i. We then de˝ne Γ i jk = e i · ∂ej ∂xk and Γ j ik = −ei · ∂ej ∂xk . These are the Christo˙el symbols of the second kind (which have 27 components). 20 35

# Page 26^page=26
Covariant differentiation in terms of Christoffel symbols Covariant di˙erentiation in terms of Christo˙el symbols If we re-write the covariant derivatives using Christo˙el symbols, we get Ai,k = ∂Ai ∂xk − Γ j ikAj, Ai ,k = ∂Ai ∂xk + Γi jkAj. The Christo˙el symbol of the second kind are Γi jk = e i · ∂ej ∂xk and Γ j ik = −ei · ∂ej ∂xk . 21 35

# Page 27^page=27
Back to a fixed basis Back to a ˝xed basis Once more, covariant derivatives are de˝ned by Ai,k = ∂Ai ∂xk − Γ j ikAj, Ai ,k = ∂Ai ∂xk + Γi jkAj. We have seen that, if the basis is ˝xed , then the Christo˙el symbols vanish: Γ i jk = e i · ∂ej ∂xk = 0. Then the covariant derivatives Ai,k and Ai ,k reduce simply to ∂Ai,k = ∂Ai ∂xk and ∂A i ,k = ∂Ai ∂xk . 22 35

# Page 28^page=28
Γ i jk as expansion coefficients Christo˙el symbols as expansion coe˚cients We will now show that Γi jk are the expansion coe˚cients of the vector ∂ej ∂xk with respect to the basis e1, e2, e3. That is ∂ej ∂xk = Γ 1 jke1 + Γ2 jke2 + Γ3 jke3 = Γ i jkei. To show this, let the following be the expansion of this vector: ∂ej ∂xk = Ai jkei. Let us show that Ai jk = Γi jk. 23 35

# Page 29^page=29
Γ i jk as expansion coefficients- Part 2 Christo˙el symbols as expansion coe˚cients To ˝nd these coe˚cients, we take the dot product of both sides of the equation with the dual basis vector em: e m · ∂ej ∂xk = e m · (Ai jkei) Since em · ei = δm i , we get: e m · ∂ej ∂xk = Ai jkδm i = Am jk. Therefore Ai jk = e i · ∂ej ∂xk while Γ i jk = e i · ∂ej ∂xk Consequently, Ai jk = Γi jk, as required. 24 35

# Page 30^page=30
Christoffel symbols of first kind Christo˙el symbols of ˝rst kind We just showed that Γi jk are the expansion coe˚cients of the vector ∂ej ∂xk with respect to the basis e1, e2, e3. That is ∂ej ∂xk = Γ 1 jke1 + Γ2 jke2 + Γ3 jke3 = Γ i jkei. We can also expand the vector ∂ej ∂xk with respect to the dual basis e1, e2, e3. The new coe˚cients are denoted by Γijk. That is ∂ej ∂xk = Γijke i =⇒ Γijk = ei · ∂ej ∂xk . These new symbols are called the Christo˙el symbols of the ˝rst kind . 25 35

# Page 31^page=31
Definitions: Two types of Christoffel Symbol De˝nitions. Christo˙el symbols of second kind : Γi jk = e i · ∂ej ∂xk . Christo˙el symbols of ˝rst kind : Γijk = ei · ∂ej ∂xk . 26 35

# Page 32^page=32
Christoffel symbols and metric tensors Christo˙el symbols and metric tensors The Christo˙el symbols can be expressed in terms of the metric tensors . Christo˙el symbols of second kind Γ i jk = e i · ∂ej ∂xk =⇒ ∂ej ∂xk = Γ i jkei. Christo˙el symbols of ˝rst kind ∂ej ∂xk = Γijke i =⇒ Γijk = ei · ∂ej ∂xk . We can then write Γijk = ei · ∂ej ∂xk = ei · Γ ℓ jkeℓ = (ei · eℓ)Γ ℓ jk = giℓΓ ℓ jk. 27 35

# Page 33^page=33
Christoffel symbols and metric tensors - Part 2 Christo˙el symbols and metric tensors Similarly, we can write Γ i jk = e i · ∂ej ∂xk = e i · Γℓjke ℓ = (e i · e ℓ)Γℓjk = giℓΓℓjk. Hence, Christo˙el symbols of the ˝rst and second kind are related via the metric tensor: Γijk = giℓΓ ℓ jk, Γ i jk = giℓΓℓkj. 28 35

# Page 34^page=34
Summary: Christoffel Symbols and the met- ric tensor Summary: Christo˙el Symbols and the metric tensor Christo˙el symbols of second kind Γi jk = e i · ∂ej ∂xk . Christo˙el symbols of ˝rst kind Γijk = ei · ∂ej ∂xk . Christo˙el symbols of the ˝rst and second kind are related via the metric tensor Γijk = giℓΓ ℓ jk, Γ i jk = giℓΓℓkj. 29 35

# Page 35^page=35
Symmetry of Christoffel symbols Symmetry of Christo˙el symbols The Christo˙el symbols Γi jk and Γijk are symmetric in the indices j and k. That is Γijk = Γikj, and Γ i jk = Γ i kj. In fact, Γijk = ei · ∂ej ∂xk = ∂r ∂xi · ∂ ∂xk ∂r ∂xj ( ei = ∂r ∂xi ) = ∂r ∂xi · ∂ ∂xj ∂r ∂xk ︸ ︷︷ ︸ re-order = ei · ∂ek ∂xj = Γikj. 30 35

# Page 36^page=36
Symmetry of Christoffel symbols- Part 2 Symmetry of Christo˙el symbols Simirly, we can show Γ i jk = e i · ∂ej ∂xk is symmetric in the indices j and k. That is Γ i jk = Γ i kj. 31 35

# Page 37^page=37
Christoffel symbols are not tensors Christo˙el symbols are not tensors We now show that the Christo˙el symbols are not tensors. Let us check how they transform under rotation of a coordinate system. We have Γ ′ ijk = e ′ i · ∂e′ j ∂x′k = (Lℓ i′eℓ) · ∂ ∂x′k (Lm j′ em) (ek = L m k′ em) = (Lℓ i′eℓ) · ( ∂ ∂xn (Lm j′ em) ∂xn ∂x′k ) (Chain rule ) = (Lℓ i′eℓ) · ( ∂ ∂xn (Lm j′ em)Ln k′) ( ∂xn ∂x′k = L n k′) . 32 35

# Page 38^page=38
Christoffel symbols are not tensors-Part 2 Christo˙el symbols are not tensors So far, we have Γ ′ ijk = (L ℓ i′eℓ) · ( ∂ ∂xn (L m j′ em)L n k′) = (L ℓ i′eℓ) · ( L m j′ ∂em ∂xn Ln k′ + em ∂Lm j′ ∂xn Ln k′) = L ℓ i′Lm j′ Ln k′ ( eℓ · ∂em ∂xn ) ︸ ︷︷ ︸ Γℓmn +L ℓ i′L n k′ ∂Lm j′ ∂xn (eℓ · em) ︸ ︷︷ ︸ gℓm = L ℓ i′Lm j′ Ln k′Γℓmn + Lℓ i′Ln k′ ∂Lm j′ ∂xn gℓm. The above is not any of the tensor transformation laws. Thus the Christo˙el symbol of the ˝rst kind is not a tensor. 33 35

# Page 39^page=39
Christoffel symbols are not tensors - Part 2 Christo˙el symbols are not tensors Similarly, we can show that the transformation law of the Christo˙el symbol of the second kind is given by Γ i jk′ = L i′ ℓ L m j′ L n k′Γℓ mn + Li′ mLn k′ ∂Lm j′ ∂xn , and thus the Christo˙ell symbol of the second kind is also not a tensor. 34 35
